arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Hawaii's attorney argued the apology resolution was a simple apology and did not repeal prior laws.
The Office of Hawaiian Affairs attorney argued three federal laws give the state absolute title to the lands.
Justice Ginsburg asked why the Court needs to decide the issue if the resolution has no substantive effect.
Justice Alito asked if the legislature could impose a moratorium on land transfers to promote reconciliation.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The dispute centers on whether a 1993 congressional apology resolution created a federal obligation. Hawaii claims the resolution did not alter state land rights. The Office of Hawaiian Affairs claims the resolution protects Native Hawaiian interests in ceded lands.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Hawaii wants the Court to confirm the state can sell its public lands.
The Office of Hawaiian Affairs wants the Court to protect Native Hawaiian interests in those lands.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines if a congressional apology can restrict state control over public lands. It defines the scope of federal obligations regarding Native Hawaiian land claims. It clarifies the legal effect of symbolic congressional resolutions on property rights.
